episode_title: Rethinking Neurology: From Broad Diagnoses to Targeted Treatments

real_qa.q: What are the most promising developments in neurology research and treatment today?
real_qa.r: Genetic therapy is the biggest development, with researchers finding genetic causes to diseases previously unknown to be genetic in origin. The application of genetic therapies is huge and will only grow in the future, enabling treatment of formerly untreatable genetic diseases like spinal muscular atrophy and breakthrough treatments for Alzheimer's disease.

real_qa.q: What are the unique challenges in conducting clinical trials for neurology research?
real_qa.r: Key challenges include finding qualified patients who want to participate and meet trial criteria, while also ensuring they are not already well-controlled on existing treatments—changing regimens may be disadvantageous. Additionally, rare neurological diseases are becoming more common in trials but their rarity makes patient recruitment difficult, requiring the right fit between clinical need and inclusion/exclusion criteria.

real_qa.q: How is CTI Clinical Trials expanding its site network and what is the long-term growth plan?
real_qa.r: CTI plans to add one to two new sites per year over the next five to ten years to build a national site network across North America, with potential expansion to Australia, Europe, and Asia. The expansion includes both acquisitive approaches—acquiring existing high-performing sites—and building new sites from scratch, with Michigan being the second major site after the Cincinnati-based Clinical Research Center.
real_qa.requete: CTI Clinical Trials site network expansion 2024

real_qa.q: What is the advantage of CTI combining CRO services with its own clinical research sites?
real_qa.r: When CTI is both the CRO and the site for a study, contracting can be completed very quickly since it occurs within the organization, allowing studies to launch much faster and enrollment to be completed at an extremely high rate. This integration provides efficiencies across all steps of the pathway, benefiting sponsors with faster startup, more cost-effective studies, and better enrollment and data quality.
real_qa.requete: CRO clinical research site integration benefits

real_qa.q: How is neurology moving toward more targeted diagnosis and treatment similar to oncology?
real_qa.r: Neurology is subdividing diseases into more specific categories only when there are different treatments available—for example, multiple sclerosis now has five or six distinct types based on treatment differences, and developmental epileptic encephalopathies are being subdivided into SC1 and SC8A mutations, each with specific targeted drugs. This mirrors how oncology evolved from treating all breast cancers the same to distinguishing estrogen-positive, progesterone-positive, and HER2-positive subtypes.
real_qa.requete: neurology targeted diagnosis genetic mutations epilepsy

He began clinical research approximately 11 years ago while maintaining his clinical practice, combining patient care with research opportunities. He leads the newly established Clinical Research Center Michigan site, which joined CTI's expanding site network.

transcript_full: Welcome to Moving Medicine Forward, a podcast by CTI Clinical Trials. I'm your host, Jeremy Schran, and on today's episode, I'm joined by Matthew Holtzman, Medical Director, and Tim Schroeder, Executive Chairman and Founder of CTI, for a conversation about rapidly changing landscape of neurology research and the continued growth of CTI's clinical research site network. We'll explore some of the breakthrough shaping neurology, the unique challenges of conducting clinical trials in this space, and how CTI's expansion into Michigan is creating new opportunities for collaboration, patient recruitment, and innovative research. Let's dive right in. Welcome to the podcast, Tim and Dr. Holtzman. We're so happy to have you here today. My pleasure. Let's start off, Dr. Holtzman, with you. Can you introduce yourself to our listeners and share a bit about your background and your role at CTI? Sure. My name's Matt Holtzman. I'm a neurologist. I started off my career at the University of Michigan, medical school there. And I did my neurology residency at the University of Iowa. I then followed that up with a fellowship in EMG and EEG, or what they call clinical neurophysiology. I started getting into clinical research about 11 years ago, and I was doing that as a sideline to my clinical practice. And I was basically combining the two. I would draw from my clinical practice and give my own personal patients the opportunity to join into clinical trials where the fit was right for them. And it kind of grew from there, and I found it really exciting to always be on the cutting edge of what was coming new in science and what some of the new thoughts were in different disease processes. You have an extensive experience in neurology. What initially drew you to the field and what has kept you passionate about it throughout your career? Well, the one thing about neurology that's different than just about any other area of medicine is what we call localization. That is, if I can see one problem, say the left side of your body is weak, we can therefore deduce where in the brain the problem is. If someone's weak in the lower half of their body, we can deduce that the problem would probably be coming from the cervical spinal cord. So being able to localize and use the circuitry of the nervous system is something that's really unique to neurology and sort of the logic of it. So that was what drew me in. And then the actual diseases were really exciting. Stroke, Parkinson's, epilepsy, they kind of are different than what you see in regular medicine. Because when a patient in medicine is in distress, they're short of breath, their heart's beating really fast, they're sweating. Neurology patients in distress don't display any of those signs. They show neurologic signs instead, which can often be paradoxical. So kind of having that unique responsibility to a theoretical knowledge that was atypical to the rest of medicine was kind of exciting. You mentioned being on the cutting edge of the science. From your perspective, how has neurology research changed over the last decade? Neurology research has exploded over the last decade, and we are now doing things with diseases we never dreamed were possible. We're now able to treat genetic diseases in neurology that didn't have treatments before, and some of which were death sentences. Diseases like spinal muscular atrophy were making huge inroads into a disease like Alzheimer's disease, which for decades, eons, was thought to be something that just came with aging. We are doing better at stopping seizures, and we're coming up with new ways to treat all sorts of neurologic diseases. So it's really exciting because the initiative coming from all of these different companies to develop these novel drugs has expanded everything we know about how the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves work. What are some of the most promising developments you're seeing today in neurology research and treatment development? That's a great question. I think genetic therapy are probably the biggest thing. We're finding genetic causes to diseases we didn't even know were genetic in origin. I think that what we're doing with genetic therapies is huge, and it's only going to grow in the future. So neurology often presents unique challenges for clinical trial design and execution. What are some of the considerations researchers and sponsors need to keep in mind when developing these programs? I would say one of the issues is finding recruitment, finding patients who, A, want to be in a clinical trial and qualify, but also who are not already well-controlled on the regimen that they're on. There are certain diseases where we have patients that are very stable and they don't necessarily need to try something new or different, and it may be disadvantageous to them to do so. So always trying to find the right fit for a trial, which includes inclusion and exclusion criteria, but also clinical need is a big thing. There's been a huge rise lately in clinical trials for rare diseases. Those are becoming much more popular in the research space. And of course, rare diseases being rare it can be hard to find patients to recruit for those trials There a growing interest in therapies involving psychedelics and other controlled substances for neurological and psychiatric conditions How do you see the research evolving over the next several years? Well, I think the research is going to become far more mainstream. I think that we've already done the proof of concept for a lot of these controlled substances, a lot of these psychedelics. I think we've already proven some of the initial benefit. We need the larger trials. And I think that there's really no shortage of pathology out there, especially in certain populations like people who've experienced PTSD and things like that, as well as patients with refractory conditions that are not treated easily by our routine oral therapies. I think that there's huge interest and I think there's going to be a huge payout on it. And I think we're going to find a large subset of patients who are going to hugely benefit from these therapies. Dr. Holtzman, you're from the new CRC Michigan or the Clinical Research Center Michigan. I kind of want to switch gears and talk about that site and the new site network that CTI has launched. So Tim, what made Michigan the right location for CTI's newest research site? I would say as always, Jeremy, it's about the people. We've made it a priority having a single site for the last 10 plus years. We've seen huge advantages opening up, whether it be to our sponsors, be to research subjects, or even our own team members, having a site, in addition to having a laboratory network and a global CRO, really offers some advantages. We have been on the lookout for the last several years of adding to our site network. And we've thought of that two ways. One is acquisitive, where you find a site that's out there performing extremely well, and you try to see, would there be an interest in joining? The other would be, do you build sites from scratch? Hardworking, passionate about research, and frankly, ones that I think right away saw the benefit of combining the two organizations together. So for us, it was a no-brainer. And then it becomes, let's understand how they do their work and let's understand who they do it for. I think there a few gray areas What we offer are some areas of research that hadn been one of CTI emphasis especially neurology And so what we can do is I think we can partner with the site in Ohio and we can recruit more patients from there because we have a larger geographic and diverse base to draw from And so with having a department that specializes in recruitment, where it's not just based on my clinical practice, but where we have a whole department dedicated to that, I think it'll make us far more competitive in recruiting patients, especially in some of the more rare diseases. Tim, how can the two locations work together in ways that ultimately benefit patients and sponsors?
